$comment: Fixture #4: the G2 milestone island, LIVE against demo-app's /island/dashboard. Charts through `#[js_extern]` and live data over SSE feeding compiled-Rust signals. Every number below is MEASURED off the running app or computed from the host's own ranking rule, not predicted. See `$landed` for the four ways the island that shipped differs from the shape this was scaffolded against, and which expectation each one moved.
name: dashboard
$events: The DEFAULT bootstrap, unlike /island/search. The dashboard delegates no handler of its own: its only input is the server's stream, which is not a delegated event. So the page carries the `BOOTSTRAP` constant's `["click"]` and this fixture proves the negative -- an island with no handlers does not cause the event list to shrink or vanish.
sourceShape: signal acme = start(0); .. signal echo = start(4);   // five prices, in cents
for row in movers([acme, bolt, crux, dyad, echo]) {
`movers` is declared once per target. The server's returns the opening prices in
slot order with nothing moved, which is exactly what the browser's FIRST run
answers, and that is what makes the markup it adopts the markup it would have
built. The browser's also reads all five signals, which is the subscription: a
tick that writes one price re-runs the loop, which re-ranks the rows and pushes
a new series at the chart.
THE LOOP IS NOT KEYED, and that is the headline finding of this fixture. See

stream.$what: The SSE feed the island subscribes to. `interact.mjs` installs a stubbed EventSource in the jsdom realm and pushes exactly the frames below, so the run is deterministic: no real connection, no real timer, and the same ticks in the same order every time.
stream.$whyStubbed: Three reasons, and only the first is convenience. (1) The real endpoint holds the connection open, so a harness reading it must bound itself. (2) A stub can push a MALFORMED frame, which a live feed will not produce to order and which is the only way to measure what a bad tick does. (3) The island's own resilience is a property of the island, not of the transport, so driving it directly is measuring the right thing.
stream.$url: MEASURED: `demo-app/island/dashboard.rs` FEED. The stub asserts the island opened exactly this url.
stream.$eventName: A NAMED SSE event, registered with `addEventListener("tick", ..)`. The framework agent's curl check records `event: tick` on the wire, so a stub dispatching only `message` would be driving nothing.
stream.$payload: One frame carries ONE row, not the whole list: {slot, symbol, price, delta}. `slot` is the index into SYMBOLS, which is the only table and both halves read it.
stream.$hostRule: What a frame does, from `demo-app/src/island-rt.mjs` `dash_sink`: set moved[slot] = delta, re-sort `ranked` by |moved| DESCENDING with ties broken by slot ASCENDING, then write prices[slot] = price. The write is what re-runs the list. `moved` PERSISTS across ticks, which is why a row that moved three ticks ago still shows its delta and still holds its rank.

ticks.$: 1. The framework agent's own id-0 frame, kept so this fixture and their curl check are driving the same bytes. CRUX moves, so it ranks first and everything else keeps slot order.

2. THE REGRESSION FRAME. DYAD 4310 -> 4460 is the exact transition that exposed the keyed bug: keyed, this row re-ordered correctly and went on reading 4310 for ever. If this fixture ever reads 4310 here, keying has come back and the list is lying about prices again.

3. A TIE on |delta|: ACME moves -150 and DYAD already holds +150. The host breaks ties by slot ascending, so ACME (slot 0) must rank above DYAD (slot 3). A ranking that is not a function of the moves alone shows up here and nowhere else.

4. THE MALFORMED FRAME. Truncated JSON, so `JSON.parse` throws inside the listener. Not a transport error: this is a well-formed SSE frame carrying a body the island cannot decode, which is the failure a real feed actually produces. See interact.mjs section 6 for what a browser does with a throwing listener and why the stub reproduces it.
5. RECOVERY, on the far side of the failure. ECHO takes the top rank with the largest move so far, which re-orders the whole list and proves the island is still both listening and ranking.

stream.$expectedRows: What the list must read after each frame, DERIVED from $hostRule rather than observed and then written down. Each entry is [symbol, price, delta] in rendered order. Computed here so a disagreement is between the island and the RULE, not between the island and whatever it happened to do the first time.
stream.$nullIsTheErrorFrame: The `null` at index 3 is the malformed frame: the list must be UNCHANGED from the row before it. Spelled as null rather than by repeating row 2, so the fixture cannot accidentally assert a coincidence -- interact.mjs reads null as `identical to the previous expectation`.
stream.$expectedClasses: `trend(delta)` in the island source: `mover up` above zero, `mover down` below, plain `mover` at zero. Asserted separately from the text because the class is a CONDITIONAL ATTRIBUTE on the row's root, and an attribute that stopped updating would leave the text correct -- the exact half a text-only assertion misses.

chart.$what: The chart library the island declares with `#[js_extern]`, and what the island did to it. Asserted as an ordered trace in the records the recorder itself writes, which are the records contract/fixtures/js-extern/vectors.json is made of.

delivery.$resolved: Nothing is stubbed and nothing is substituted. demo-app serves THIS SUITE'S OWN RECORDER at /demo/chart-lib.js -- `include_str!("../../contract/fixtures/js-extern/chart-lib.mjs")` in dom.rs -- and the page's import map resolves `topcoat-chart` to it. So the module the island calls into IS the module the js-extern vectors were recorded from, it stages like any other served module, and this fixture reads its trace by importing the SAME staged instance through the run's `moduleFor`. That removes the whole class of doubt about whether a fake resembled the real declaration surface: it is the same file.
delivery.$importMapFirst: `topcoat-chart` is the first import map entry that is not the runtime, the host module or an island. Worth pinning: it is the mechanism by which a REAL chart library takes this one's place without the island's declarations changing.

chart.$emitted:
The JavaScript the backend emitted for the five declarations, from the framework agent's report:
  import { Chart as ext$Chart$h6fde69f85c63bdae } from "topcoat-chart";
  new ext$Chart$...(document.querySelector(".dash-chart"), { kind: "line", span: 5 })
  new EventSource("/demo/ticks")
  feed.addEventListener("tick", ..)
  __rt.dash_chart().update({ acme: .., bolt: .., crux: .., dyad: .., echo: .. })
Three of the five are GLOBAL-SCOPE declarations (EventSource, document.querySelector, addEventListener) and emit no import at all; only the chart library is imported. That is the wave-5 `g` flag doing its job, and it is why the trace below has exactly one construction from a module binding.

expectedShapes.$: Construction, once, during hydration and before any tick. `via` is the import binding the descriptor named and is the ONLY thing JS-EXTERN.md's new-named and new-default differ on, so it is the whole record of which binding was taken.
The hydration update. The chart is fed inside the list's effect, so its first run pushes the opening series before a single tick has arrived.
tick 5, the recovery. There is NO entry for tick 4.

chart.$noRecordForTheErrorTick: SIX records for FIVE frames: one construction and five updates, where five frames plus a hydration run would be six updates. The missing one is the assertion. A malformed frame must not reach the chart, because a library handed a partly decoded series draws a WRONG chart rather than failing -- the quiet outcome. The count is what catches it, so the trace is compared for length as well as position.
chart.$expectedSeries: The series each `update` must carry, in call order: the opening prices, then one per good tick. A `#[repr(C)]` struct crosses as an object keyed by its RUST FIELD NAMES, which is why these are `acme`..`echo` and not an array -- and asserting the keys is asserting that half of the value model. Note the series is the CURRENT price of every symbol, not a delta: a tick writes one signal and the loop reads all five.

expected.$seeds: Arity 0. The five signals are declared inside the `view!` body, so nothing is seeded through `data-ts`, which the served mount carries as `[]`.
expected.$keys: Six, and this is the first fixture where the island's LIST IS SERVER-RENDERED: the root plus one per row. Every earlier island's list started empty and was filled by the client, so this is the first time hydration has to adopt repeated rows rather than create them.
expected.$templates: The island's own root and the `<li>` the `for` body declares.
expected.$islandTemplate: MEASURED now, not predicted: the framework agent's report records the island's own template FIRST. `search` left the same field as an unverified scaffold assumption; this one is confirmed.
expected.$hydrateMutations: Zero, and it is a stronger claim here than anywhere else in this suite. The browser's first effect run must answer the SAME five rows, in the same order, with the same numbers the server wrote -- because the host starts at ranked [0,1,2,3,4] with moved all zero and the prices come from the signals' own initialisers. Any disagreement between the two `movers` implementations shows up as a mutation during hydration.
expected.$clickMutations: Not applicable: this island's updates are driven by the stream, and the mutation claims are made in interact.mjs against the list's own content.
expected.$openingRows: What the SERVER sent, verbatim from the captured markup, and therefore also what the client's first run must produce. Asserted before any tick so that a hydration which silently rebuilt the list is caught by content as well as by mutation count.
$notKeyed: THE HEADLINE FINDING, and this fixture asserts the OPPOSITE of what it was scaffolded to assert.
The brief asked for a keyed `for` and keyed node identity across reorder. It was written that
way, and running it showed the design is wrong for THIS list. `view_abi::push_keyed` hands back
the node a key contributed last time and DISCARDS the row just built, text included. So the list
re-ordered correctly and then rendered its first values for ever: MEASURED, a row read 4310
after a tick that set it to 4460, which is tick 2 of this fixture's stream.
Keying is right for a row whose text does not change, or whose changing parts are reactive holes
of the row's own template. Neither holds here -- every tick changes a price and a move -- and
per-row reactive holes are not reachable, because a `$( )` cannot carry a free function call.
So the loop rebuilds five short rows per tick and the prices are right.
WHAT THIS FIXTURE THEREFORE ASSERTS: that the rows are REPLACED on every tick, and that the text
is correct. It explicitly does NOT assert node identity across a reorder, and it must not: that
assertion would pass for the broken keyed version and fail for the correct one, which is exactly
backwards. The identity check is INVERTED instead -- see interact.mjs section 4 -- so that if
keying comes back silently, this fixture notices.
WHAT WOULD HAVE TO CHANGE for keying to be right here: `push_keyed` would have to update the
retained node from the freshly built row, or the row's changing parts would have to become
reactive holes of its own template. Until one of those, keyed identity is not a property this
list can have AND be correct.
WAVE 6 RESOLVED IT, AND THE ANSWER IS THAT NEITHER CHANGE IS COMING. `push_keyed` stays
identity-only, this list is not re-keyed, and the inverted assertion above STANDS with a second
cause added. Three findings, from the backend's wave-6 report item 1:
K1. There is no disposal bug behind this. A plain `( )` row hole is `Fill::Once` and emits a
bare `_$insert` with no effect at all; a `$( )` hole IS an effect but is owned by the
ISLAND, not the row, because a Rust loop opens no reactive scope. The rule is therefore
sharper than 'keyed is for static rows': a keyed row's changing parts must be reactive
holes OF THE ROW'S OWN TEMPLATE, and a plain `( )` hole in a keyed row is written once to
a node that is then thrown away. That is this list exactly.
K2. Both repairs are unsound. Re-running the fills against the cached node silently
DUPLICATES an anchored child hole -- upstream's `insert` seeds `current = []` when
`initial` is undefined, so a second text node lands before the anchor on every render.
Morphing the cached node from the fresh one cannot see `HoleKind::Event` or
`HoleKind::Property`, and there is no DOM implementation in this tree to verify a morph
against: the three stubs that exist disagree about where a hole's value even lives.
K3. THE DECIDING ONE. Even a perfect fix does not move corpus family 13 to MATCH. The
reference is solid's `<For>`, which clones a row's template once per row EVER; ours is an
eager Rust loop that clones once per row PER RENDER, before `push_keyed` is reached. The
divergence is the loop, not the reconcile, which is what the standing rule is named after:
`keyed-list-vs-a-rust-loop`, `examples/dom-tests/deltas.json`. Family 13 is ATTRIBUTED for
a structural reason that outlives any version of `push_keyed`, and
`contract/fixtures/l2-status.json` records it as such.
So the standing OUT-list entry for keyed `for` is not a deferral waiting on a fix. It is a
design consequence of `for` being a Rust loop. interact.mjs's header carries the full flip
history; read it before flipping this assertion a third time.

$landed.$what: The differences between what this fixture predicted while pending and what landed. Recorded because a scaffold quietly edited to match what shipped proves nothing.
divergences: KEYED -> UNKEYED, and it inverted the fixture's central assertion. See `expected.$notKeyed`. This is the one divergence that moved an expectation rather than a detail, and it moved it to the opposite claim.

THE LIST IS SERVER-RENDERED. The scaffold predicted an empty list filled by the first tick, as `search`'s is, and therefore one key. What shipped renders all five rows on the server, so `expected.keys` is six and hydration has to ADOPT repeated rows -- a case no earlier fixture reaches.

A FRAME CARRIES ONE ROW, NOT THE LIST. The scaffold predicted `{movers: [[symbol, change], ..]}`. The feed sends `{slot, symbol, price, delta}` and the RANKING is the host's, recomputed per tick from a persistent `moved` table. So the expected rows are derived from the host's documented rule rather than read off the frame, which is a stronger test: it checks the ranking, not just the rendering.

SELECTORS. `.chart` -> `.dash-chart`, and a row is three spans (`.mover-symbol`, `.mover-price`, `.mover-delta`) rather than one text node. Nothing moved but the strings, because every selector was already read out of this file.
